The Common ling (Molva molva) is a large-bodied gadiform inhabiting the continental shelf of the North Atlantic, where it attains a considerable ultimate total length of 200 cm [Li = 200 cm]. Field surveys indicate that individuals typically reach this maximum after a prolonged growth period, a pattern common among slow-growing demersal piscivores. Females in particular undergo an extensive juvenile phase, during which somatic growth is prioritised over reproductive development. The onset of reproductive capability is marked by a total length at puberty of 90 cm [Lp = 90 cm], corresponding roughly to the size at which individuals are recruited into the spawning stock. This length threshold, estimated from the examination of gonadal maturation stages in trawl-caught specimens, aligns closely with values reported for other large lotid species. The transition from the immature to the mature phase appears to be closely linked to energetic condition, with fish that experience higher prey availability reaching puberty at slightly smaller sizes. Data from long-term monitoring programmes suggest that the age at which this length is attained varies with local temperature regimes and food supply.

Reproductive output in Common ling has been documented from studies of gravid females captured during the spawning season. Individuals maintained at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] exhibit an extraordinarily high maximum annual production, with estimates derived from both batch fecundity counts and spawning frequency. A typical gravid female produces approximately 164,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 164,000 eggs per spawning event], and multiple spawning events occur across the breeding season. The spawning frequency has been recorded as approximately one event per day [F_R_i = approximately one event per day] under controlled experimental conditions at this stable thermal regime. This combination yields a remarkably high reproductive capacity, reflective of a species that invests heavily in offspring numbers rather than parental care. The pelagic eggs are released into the water column, where they drift with currents, a strategy that disperses the progeny widely and reduces density-dependent competition among larvae.

The life cycle of Common ling begins with the production of small, buoyant eggs, which upon fertilisation give rise to a yolk-sac larva following eclosion. The newly emerged larva possesses a wet weight at birth of 0.0005 grams [Wwb = 0.0005 grams], a minimal mass that necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding. This value is consistent with the size of the eggs, which measure approximately 1 mm in diameter, a dimension typical of pelagic spawning gadoids. The tiny prolarvae rely initially on their endogenous yolk reserves, absorbing this nutritional store during the first few days post-hatch. First exogenous feeding coincides with the opening of the mouth and the differentiation of the retina, enabling the larva to detect and capture planktonic prey. Larval mortality during this period is extremely high, a common feature in teleosts that produce large numbers of small offspring. The yolk-sac stage lasts for a brief interval before the larva enters the actively swimming, planktonic feeding phase, where growth rates depend heavily on prey concentrations.

As females mature and approach the onset of reproductive activity, they undergo substantial somatic growth, accumulating the tissue reserves necessary to support gametogenesis. At the point of sexual maturation, defined by the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in the ovary, the wet weight at puberty reaches approximately 4000 grams [Wwp = approximately 4000 grams]. This mass represents a considerable energetic investment and is typically attained several years after the individual achieves the threshold length for puberty, reflecting the time required to build up sufficient body condition. In fully mature, reproductively active females, the ultimate female wet weight attains a value of 47,000 grams [Wwi = 47,000 grams], a size that corresponds closely to the asymptotic mass predicted by the length–weight relationship derived from the ultimate length. Records of exceptionally large specimens indicate that this mass is reached only by the oldest and most fecund individuals in the population, which dominate the annual reproductive output.

Longevity records for Molva molva, compiled from tag-recapture programmes and otolith ageing studies, indicate that the lifespan in this species is extensive, with the oldest documented individuals persisting for up to 25 years [am = up to 25 years] at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This maximum longevity has been recorded in populations inhabiting cooler waters at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], where metabolic rates are lower and the pace of life is slowed relative to warmer environments. The extended lifespan is consistent with a life-history strategy that delays reproduction until a relatively large body size is achieved, a pattern that allows iteroparous females to spawn repeatedly over many seasons. Such a prolonged reproductive window compensates for the high pre-adult mortality characteristic of pelagic-spawning gadoids. Comparative data for other large-bodied members of the Lotidae suggest that the observed age of 25 years is near the upper bound for the family, though captures of very old individuals are rare due to fishing pressure on mature cohorts.
